headline: Prime Minister hails £12bn RWE and KKR offshore wind investment for Norfolk

terms.meaning: Wind turbines built in the sea, where winds are stronger and steadier than on land.
A unit of power equal to a billion watts, enough for hundreds of thousands of homes.
Money put into a project now in the hope of a return later.

levels.headline: Prime Minister hails £12bn RWE and KKR offshore wind investment for Norfolk
levels.body:
The Government announced on 11 November that the energy company RWE and the investment firm KKR will together invest £12 billion in the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind projects off Norfolk. Ministers say it is possibly the largest investment of its kind in UK history.
The wind farms are expected to be operating by 2030. The announcement came as Prime Minister Andy Burnham prepared to travel to the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, which runs from 9 to 20 November.
The same Government release also highlighted Berwick Bank, off Scotland's east coast, which it says could become the world's largest offshore wind farm at full capacity, supplying more than 6% of current UK electricity demand.
Background: RWE and KKR agreed their partnership on the Norfolk Vanguard projects after a record auction in which the UK secured 8.4 gigawatts of new offshore wind. The £12 billion figure and the 'largest ever' claim come from the Government's own release, and no independent confirmation was found.
levels.why: Large energy projects shape bills, jobs and the UK's reliance on imported fuel.

levels.headline: £12bn offshore wind deal announced as PM heads to COP31
levels.body:
RWE and KKR will invest £12 billion in two Norfolk offshore wind farms, Vanguard West and Vanguard East, the Government said on 11 November. It described the sum as possibly the biggest investment of its kind in UK history.
The farms should be running by 2030. Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the news just before travelling to the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, which lasts until 20 November.
The release also pointed to Berwick Bank, off Scotland's east coast. At full capacity the Government says it could be the world's largest offshore wind farm, meeting over 6% of today's UK electricity demand.
The partnership between RWE and KKR follows a record auction that secured 8.4 gigawatts of offshore wind capacity. The headline figure and the 'largest ever' description are the Government's own, and could not be checked against independent reports.
levels.why: Where electricity comes from affects household bills and the country's energy security.

levels.headline: Government says £12bn will be invested in two Norfolk wind farms
levels.body:
The Government says the energy firm RWE and investment company KKR will invest £12 billion in two offshore wind farms off Norfolk, called Vanguard West and Vanguard East. Ministers believe it may be the biggest investment of its kind in UK history.
The turbines are due to be working by 2030. The announcement came on 11 November, just before Prime Minister Andy Burnham went to the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.
The Government also mentioned Berwick Bank off the Scottish coast. When complete, it says, the wind farm could be the largest of its kind in the world and supply more than 6% of the electricity the UK uses now.
The companies teamed up after a record government auction for offshore wind. The £12 billion total comes from the Government rather than an independent source.
levels.why: More home-grown power can mean steadier prices and more jobs.

levels.headline: £12 billion for new wind farms off the Norfolk coast
levels.body:
The Government has announced that two companies, RWE and KKR, plan to spend £12 billion on two wind farms in the sea off Norfolk. They are called Vanguard West and Vanguard East. Ministers say it could be the biggest deal of its kind the UK has ever seen.
The wind farms should start producing power by 2030. Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the news on 11 November, before he left for COP31, a big international climate meeting in Türkiye.
The Government also talked about Berwick Bank, off the east coast of Scotland. It says this could one day be the largest offshore wind farm in the world, powering more than 6% of what the UK uses today.
The £12 billion figure comes from the Government, and we could not find anyone else confirming it.
levels.why: Making power at home helps protect the UK from price shocks abroad.

levels.headline: Two firms plan £12bn of wind farms off Norfolk
levels.body:
Two companies, RWE and KKR, plan to spend £12 billion building wind farms in the sea off Norfolk. The Government announced it on 11 November and says it may be the biggest investment of its kind in UK history.
The wind farms are called Vanguard West and Vanguard East. They should be making electricity by 2030. Offshore wind farms are built at sea because the wind there blows harder and more steadily than on land.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the news as he got ready to go to COP31, a world climate meeting in Türkiye. The Government also said a wind farm called Berwick Bank, off Scotland, could one day be the largest in the world.
The £12 billion figure is the Government's own number.
levels.why: Cheaper, home-made power could help keep energy bills down in future.

levels.headline: Big companies will spend £12bn on wind farms at sea
levels.body:
Two big companies, RWE and KKR, say they will spend £12 billion on two wind farms in the sea near Norfolk. The Government shared the news on 11 November. It says this may be the biggest deal like it ever in the UK.
The wind farms are called Vanguard West and Vanguard East. They are meant to be finished and working by 2030. Wind farms use the wind to spin big blades, and that makes electricity for homes and shops.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham was pleased about the news. He was about to go to COP31, a large meeting where countries talk about the climate.
The Government says another wind farm, Berwick Bank in Scotland, could one day be the biggest in the world. The £12 billion figure comes from the Government.
levels.why: Using the wind for power could help keep bills steadier and the air cleaner.

levels.headline: New wind farms at sea will cost £12 billion
levels.body:
Some big companies want to build two new wind farms in the sea near Norfolk. They will spend £12 billion, which is a huge amount of money. The Government told people about it on 11 November.
A wind farm is a group of tall machines called turbines. The wind turns their blades, and this makes electricity. At sea, the wind is stronger, so the turbines can make more power.
The farms are called Vanguard West and Vanguard East. They should be working by 2030, which is about four years away.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said he was happy about the plan. The money figure comes from the Government, so we cannot be sure others agree with it.
levels.why: Electricity made from wind does not run out, and it can help keep bills lower.

levels.headline: Two giant wind farms are planned in the sea
levels.body:
Two companies want to build wind farms in the sea. The sea is near Norfolk, in England. The plan will cost £12 billion. That is a very big pile of money.
A wind farm has tall machines called turbines. Wind pushes their blades round and round. The turning makes electricity. We use electricity for lights, phones and TVs.
The wind farms should start working in 2030. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said he was pleased. He told people the news on 11 November.
Nobody else has checked the money number yet. It was given by the Government. Wind is free and never runs out, so people like using it to make power.
levels.why: Wind power can give homes electricity without burning fuel.

levels.headline: Big wind farms will be built at sea
levels.body:
Some people want to build giant wind machines in the sea. They want to put them near a place called Norfolk. It will cost a huge amount of money. Grown-ups say it is £12 billion.
The machines are called turbines. They look like very tall fans. The wind blows and spins them. When they spin, they make electricity. Electricity makes lamps shine and lets you watch TV.
They should be ready in the year 2030. The leader of the country, called the Prime Minister, said it was good news.
The wind is free. It never runs out. So wind machines are a clever way to get power.
levels.why: Wind is a free way to make the power we need at home.

levels.headline: Giant windmills in the sea
levels.body:
Think of a windmill at the seaside, spinning in the breeze. Now think of lots of them, standing in the sea. That is what some people plan to build near a place called Norfolk.
When the wind pushes the big blades, they spin, and that makes electricity for homes and schools. It is a bit like how you make a pinwheel turn by blowing on it.
It costs a lot of money. Grown-ups say it is £12 billion. That is more pocket money than anyone could count.
The windmills should be ready in the year 2030. The wind is free, so these windmills help us make power without using up anything.
levels.why: Windmills at sea help make power in a gentle way.

headline: S&P 500 closes up about 1.3% at 7,619 as CoreWeave results and an Nvidia rebound lift tech

terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 of the biggest US-listed companies, widely used to judge the health of the stock market.
An index dominated by technology companies.
An index of 30 large American companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes up about 1.3% at 7,619 as CoreWeave results and an Nvidia rebound lift tech
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed higher on Wednesday 11 November, the last completed session, rising about 1.3% to finish at 7,619.38, according to CNBC's market coverage.
The Nasdaq Composite gained about 1.6% to close near 25,466. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about 255 points, or 0.49%, to around 52,486. One other data provider reported a larger Nasdaq gain of 2.3%, so the Nasdaq figure varies by source.
CNBC attributed the rally to strong earnings from CoreWeave and a rebound in Nvidia shares. It followed a fall on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected US inflation data, and a strong Monday 9 November in which the S&P 500 had its best day since April.
A separate CNBC article suggested a much larger fall on another date, but its date did not match the Wednesday rally and could not be verified, so it is not relied on here.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions, savings and how confident businesses feel about spending.

levels.headline: Wall Street rebounds on Wednesday as tech recovers
levels.body:
US shares rose on Wednesday 11 November, the last completed trading day. The S&P 500 closed up about 1.3% at 7,619.38, according to CNBC.
The Nasdaq Composite finished about 1.6% higher near 25,466, although another data provider put its gain at 2.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added around 255 points, or 0.49%, to close near 52,486.
CNBC said strong results from CoreWeave and a bounce in Nvidia shares drove the gains. Markets had fallen on Tuesday after a hot US inflation report, having jumped on Monday, when the S&P 500 had its best day since April.
The figures differ slightly between sources, and a separate report of a much steeper fall carried a date that did not fit, so it was left out.
levels.why: Moves in US shares can affect UK investments and pension funds.

levels.headline: US stocks climb as technology shares bounce back
levels.body:
US stocks closed higher on Wednesday 11 November, the latest completed session. The S&P 500 rose about 1.3% to 7,619.38, CNBC reported.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was up roughly 1.6% at about 25,466, though one other source gave a bigger rise of 2.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained about 255 points, or 0.49%, to near 52,486.
The gains were put down to strong results from the computing company CoreWeave and a recovery in the chip maker Nvidia. Tuesday had seen a fall after inflation came in hotter than forecast, and Monday had been the S&P 500's best day since April.
Sources differ a little on the Nasdaq figure, so it should be treated as approximate.
levels.why: Share prices show how confident investors are about the economy and company profits.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends higher as chip and computing firms recover
levels.body:
Shares in the United States rose on Wednesday 11 November, the most recent full trading day. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big companies, closed up about 1.3% at 7,619.
The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, rose about 1.6% to around 25,466. The Dow, which follows 30 large companies, was up about 0.49% at roughly 52,486.
CNBC said the rise came from good results at CoreWeave, a company that provides computing power, and from Nvidia, a chip maker, recovering some earlier losses. On Tuesday shares had fallen after prices in America rose faster than expected.
One source gave a different Nasdaq rise, so the exact figure is uncertain.
levels.why: What happens to US shares often spreads to markets around the world.

levels.headline: US share prices rise after a bumpy week
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States went up on Wednesday 11 November. The S&P 500, a measure of 500 big companies, rose by about 1.3% and closed at 7,619.
The Nasdaq, full of tech companies, went up by around 1.6%. The Dow, which follows 30 big firms, rose by about 0.49%.
CNBC reported two main reasons. A computing company called CoreWeave shared good results, and Nvidia, which makes computer chips, saw its share price bounce back. Shares had dropped the day before because prices in the shops were rising faster than people hoped.
Where sources disagreed on the Nasdaq rise, we have used the more common figure.
levels.why: Share prices can affect pensions and the money firms have to grow.

levels.headline: Shares in America go up on Wednesday
levels.body:
On Wednesday 11 November, shares in the United States went up. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, closed about 1.3% higher at 7,619.
The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology firms, rose about 1.6%. The Dow, which follows 30 large companies, rose about 0.49%.
CNBC said a company called CoreWeave, which supplies computing power, shared strong results. Nvidia, a chip maker, also recovered. Both helped shares to rise.
On Tuesday, shares had fallen because prices in America rose faster than hoped. So Wednesday won some of that back. Sources differ a little on the exact Nasdaq rise.
levels.why: Moves in share prices can affect pensions and savings.

levels.headline: American shares go up again on Wednesday
levels.body:
On Wednesday 11 November, the main list of US company shares, the S&P 500, closed 1.3% higher. A share is a small piece of a company. When more people want to buy than sell, prices rise.
The Nasdaq, a list full of technology firms, went up around 1.6%. The Dow, a list of 30 large companies, went up about 0.49%.
The rise came because a company called CoreWeave had good news about its money. Nvidia, which makes computer chips, also recovered after a bad spell.
The day before, shares had fallen. That was because prices for things in America rose faster than hoped, which made people worry.
levels.why: Changes in share prices can touch the pensions many people will rely on.

levels.headline: Share prices in America go up
levels.body:
Share prices in America went up on Wednesday. A share is a tiny slice of a company. If you own a slice, you own a little bit of that business.
The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big companies. Its prices rose by about 1.3% that day. The Nasdaq, a list with many tech firms, rose by about 1.6%. The Dow, a list of 30 firms, rose by less than 0.5%.
Two companies had good news. CoreWeave told people its results were strong. Nvidia, which makes computer chips, bounced back.
On the day before, share prices had dropped. So Wednesday helped to win some of that back.
levels.why: Share prices show how people feel about companies and can affect savings.

levels.headline: Shares go up in America
levels.body:
On Wednesday, many shares in America got more expensive. A share is a tiny piece of a company. People buy and sell them every day.
There are lists that show how a group of shares is doing. One is called the S&P 500, and it follows 500 big companies. It went up by a little over one in every hundred. Another list is called the Nasdaq, and it went up a bit more.
Shares went up because two firms had good news. One makes computer chips and the other helps big computers work. The day before, shares had gone down, so this was a bounce back.
Shares can go up and down every single day.
levels.why: Share prices rising or falling can change how safe people feel about their savings.

levels.headline: The shop where people buy bits of companies
levels.body:
Imagine a big school fair with a stall where people swap tiny bits of companies, like trading stickers. Prices go up when lots of children want a sticker, and down when few do.
On Wednesday, in America, lots of people wanted these tiny bits. So the prices went up. The big list of 500 companies went up by about one penny in every pound.
Two companies had good news, a bit like winning a sports day race, so more people wanted their stickers. The day before, prices had gone down. So Wednesday was a step back up.
Prices at the stall wobble every day.
levels.why: Prices of company shares go up and down just like swapping stickers.

headline: US inflation hotter than expected in October, raising bets on a Federal Reserve rate rise in December

terms.meaning: A measure of how much the prices of everyday goods and services rise.
Inflation leaving out food and energy, which can swing sharply.
The return investors get from lending to the US government; it affects borrowing costs.

levels.headline: US inflation hotter than expected in October, raising bets on a Federal Reserve rate rise in December
levels.body:
US consumer prices rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% economists expected, according to the report released on 10 November. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% against a forecast of 0.2%.
No official annual rate was available because last year's government shutdown left gaps in October 2025 data. Bank of America estimated annual inflation at 3.8% for the headline figure and 2.7% for core.
The 10-year Treasury yield briefly rose back above 5% before easing just below it. The Fed held its rate at 3.75% to 4% at its October meeting, and traders are now fully pricing in a quarter-point rise when it meets on 8 to 9 December. Governor Christopher Waller said a hot report could justify a half-point rise, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she saw a need for two more quarter-point increases.
levels.why: Rising US interest rates raise borrowing costs worldwide and can affect UK mortgages and markets.

levels.headline: US prices rise faster than forecast, pushing the Fed towards a rate rise
levels.body:
US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than the 0.3% forecast, the 10 November report showed. Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% against a forecast of 0.2%.
There is no official yearly figure because last year's government shutdown disrupted October 2025 data. Bank of America put annual headline inflation at an estimated 3.8% and core at 2.7%.
The 10-year Treasury yield briefly went back above 5% and then eased slightly. The Federal Reserve kept rates at 3.75% to 4% in October. Traders now fully expect a quarter-point rise on 8 to 9 December. Fed governor Christopher Waller suggested a half-point move could be justified, while Lorie Logan, president of the Dallas Fed, said she wanted two more quarter-point rises.
levels.why: Higher US rates can push up borrowing costs for governments and households elsewhere.

levels.headline: Hot US inflation figures make a December interest rate rise look certain
levels.body:
Prices in the US rose by 0.4% in October, faster than the 0.3% economists predicted. Prices excluding food and energy, known as core, rose 0.3%, against a forecast of 0.2%.
A government shutdown last year left gaps in the October 2025 figures, so there is no official annual rate. Bank of America estimated 3.8% overall and 2.7% for core.
The 10-year government bond yield briefly passed 5%. The Federal Reserve held its rate between 3.75% and 4% in October, but traders now fully expect a quarter-point rise when it meets on 8 to 9 December. Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rise could be justified, and Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan said two more quarter-point rises might be needed.
levels.why: The Fed's decisions influence interest rates and the value of money around the world.

levels.headline: US inflation comes in higher than expected, and the Fed is expected to raise rates
levels.body:
US consumer prices rose by 0.4% in October. Economists had expected 0.3%. Core prices, which leave out food and energy because they swing a lot, rose 0.3%, against 0.2% expected.
Because of a government shutdown in 2025, official yearly figures are missing. Bank of America estimates annual inflation at 3.8%, or 2.7% for core.
The yield, or return, on 10-year US government bonds briefly went above 5%. The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, kept its rate at 3.75% to 4% in October. Traders now fully expect it to raise the rate by 0.25 points on 8 to 9 December. One Fed official, Christopher Waller, said a bigger rise could be justified.
levels.why: The US sets the tone for global borrowing costs, which reach UK households too.

levels.headline: US prices rise faster than forecast, so a December rate rise looks likely
levels.body:
Prices in the United States rose by 0.4% in October, which was faster than the 0.3% experts expected. Prices rose 0.3% when food and energy were left out, against a forecast of 0.2%.
There is no official yearly figure, because a government shutdown last year left gaps in the data. Bank of America thinks prices are about 3.8% higher than a year ago.
The Federal Reserve is America's central bank, and it sets the cost of borrowing. In October it left the cost unchanged. Now traders expect it to raise the cost by a quarter of a percentage point when it meets on 8 to 9 December. A few officials think it may need to go further.
levels.why: Higher US borrowing costs can spread to other countries.

levels.headline: Prices rise faster in America, so interest rates may go up
levels.body:
Prices in the United States went up by 0.4% in October. That is more than the 0.3% experts expected. When food and energy are left out, prices rose by 0.3%, instead of the expected 0.2%.
There is no official yearly number, because a shutdown of the US government last year left gaps in the data. Bank of America guesses that prices are about 3.8% higher than a year ago.
The Federal Reserve, which sets interest rates in America, held them at 3.75% to 4% in October. Now traders expect it to raise them by a quarter of a percentage point in December. Some Fed officials think they may need to go further.
levels.why: When US interest rates rise, borrowing can become more expensive in many countries.

levels.headline: American prices go up faster, so the Fed may raise interest rates
levels.body:
Prices in America went up by 0.4% in October. People had thought it would be 0.3%, so it was a bit worse than hoped. Prices went up when food and energy were left out too, by 0.3%.
There is no official figure for the whole year. A shutdown of the government last year meant some information was missing. Bank of America thinks prices are about 3.8% higher than a year ago.
The Fed is the bank that looks after America's money. It decides how much it costs to borrow. In October it left that cost alone. Now people expect it to make borrowing cost a bit more in December, to slow rising prices.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs in America can affect prices and loans in other countries too.

levels.headline: Shop prices rose more than expected in America
levels.body:
Prices in American shops rose by 0.4% in October. This is called inflation, which means things cost more than before. Experts had thought prices would rise by 0.3%, so this was higher than they hoped.
The Fed is America's central bank. Its job is to try to keep prices steady. It can do that by changing interest rates, the extra money you pay when you borrow. If borrowing costs more, people spend less, and prices usually rise more slowly.
The Fed left its rate alone in October. Now people who buy and sell money and bonds expect it to raise the rate in December. A few Fed leaders even think it may need to go up more than once.
levels.why: Rising prices and rising interest rates can make life more expensive for families.

levels.headline: Prices climb in America, and borrowing may cost more
levels.body:
Prices in America are going up faster than people wanted. In October they rose by 0.4%. That is a small step, but experts had thought it would be a smaller one.
Prices going up is called inflation. It means your pocket money buys a little less than before. To slow it down, a bank called the Fed can make borrowing cost more. That is called raising interest rates.
The Fed did not change the cost in October. But now many people think it will raise the cost in December. A few of the Fed's leaders think it may need to do this more than once.
Raising rates can slow prices, but it can also make loans harder to pay.
levels.why: When prices rise, the cost of loans can rise too, which touches many families.

levels.headline: When sweets cost more
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweets cost 50p last month, and this month they cost a little more. Your pocket money buys fewer sweets now. That is what grown-ups call inflation.
In America, prices went up by a little more than people had guessed in October. The bank that looks after American money is called the Fed. It is like a teacher who tries to keep the playground fair.
If prices rise too fast, the Fed can make borrowing money cost more. Then people spend a bit less, and prices rise more slowly. The Fed thinks it may do this in December.
It is a bit like asking everyone to slow down in the playground.
levels.why: Rising prices mean money buys less, so leaders try to slow them down.

headline: Abu Dhabi talks between Russia and Ukraine bring a prisoner exchange but no ceasefire

terms.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting, even if the war is not over.
A region of eastern Ukraine claimed by Russia and partly held by its forces.
A person or country that helps two sides talk to each other.

levels.headline: Abu Dhabi talks between Russia and Ukraine bring a prisoner exchange but no ceasefire
levels.body:
US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia took place in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, nine months after the last round. The only concrete result reported by Euronews was a large prisoner exchange, with no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov rejected a truce, accusing Europeans of wanting one so they could deploy troops to Ukraine. He dismissed the European officials who had travelled to Abu Dhabi, saying: 'Let them sit there in the hotel.'
US officials were more positive. Marco Rubio called the talks 'very productive' and Jared Kushner said the gaps had narrowed, though he admitted: 'we are pushing a boulder uphill' towards a meeting of Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The main sticking point is territory. Moscow still demands the whole of Donbas, including areas it has failed to capture, while Kyiv refuses to give up land.
levels.why: The war shapes European security, energy prices and the cost of defence for UK taxpayers.

levels.headline: Ukraine peace talks end with prisoner swap but no truce
levels.body:
Talks between Ukraine and Russia, mediated by the United States, were held in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. They were the first in nine months. Euronews reported that the only tangible outcome was a large prisoner exchange.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov rejected a ceasefire, saying Europeans wanted one to send troops into Ukraine. He mocked the European delegates, saying: 'Let them sit there in the hotel.'
Washington sounded upbeat. Marco Rubio called the talks 'very productive', and Jared Kushner said the sides were closer, while admitting: 'we are pushing a boulder uphill' to arrange a Putin and Zelenskyy meeting.
Territory remains the main obstacle. Russia demands the entire Donbas region, which Ukraine will not give up.
levels.why: A lasting peace would change Europe's security, energy markets and public spending.

levels.headline: No ceasefire after two days of Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine held two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, the first for nine months. Euronews said a large prisoner exchange was the only concrete result.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov turned down a ceasefire. He accused European countries of wanting a truce so they could put troops in Ukraine, and said of their officials in Abu Dhabi: 'Let them sit there in the hotel.'
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks 'very productive'. Jared Kushner said the gaps had narrowed, but also said: 'we are pushing a boulder uphill' to get Putin and Zelenskyy together.
The biggest disagreement is land. Russia insists on all of the Donbas region, and Ukraine refuses.
levels.why: The outcome affects European safety and what governments spend on defence.

levels.headline: Russia and Ukraine talk in Abu Dhabi but fail to agree a ceasefire
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November for talks organised by the United States. It was their first meeting in nine months. The only real result, Euronews reported, was a large exchange of prisoners.
Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said no to a ceasefire, a pause in the fighting. He said European countries wanted one to send troops to Ukraine, and he brushed off European officials who had come to the city.
US officials spoke warmly of the talks. Marco Rubio said they were 'very productive'. But Jared Kushner said it was like pushing 'a boulder uphill' to get the two leaders into one room.
The hardest issue is land: Russia wants all of eastern Ukraine's Donbas region.
levels.why: A deal or no deal affects the safety of Europe and the price of defence and energy.

levels.headline: Russia and Ukraine hold peace talks in Abu Dhabi, but no ceasefire
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine held talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, with the United States acting as go-between. It was the first meeting in nine months.
The main result was a large swap of prisoners. A ceasefire, meaning a pause in the fighting, was not agreed. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, rejected one and said Europeans wanted it so they could send troops to Ukraine.
US officials called the talks 'very productive'. Still, one of them said it was like 'pushing a boulder uphill' to get the Russian and Ukrainian presidents together.
The big problem is land. Russia wants the whole Donbas region in eastern Ukraine, and Ukraine will not give it up.
levels.why: The war affects safety in Europe and the cost of defence and energy.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia talk again, but the fighting goes on
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia held talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. The United States helped to set them up. It was the first time in nine months that the two sides had met like this.
The only clear result was that each side let a large group of prisoners go. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said Russia did not want a ceasefire, which is a pause in the fighting. He also said European countries only wanted one so they could send soldiers to Ukraine.
American leaders said the talks were useful. Even so, one of them said it was like 'pushing a boulder uphill' to get the leaders of the two countries together.
Both sides still disagree about land in eastern Ukraine.
levels.why: Whether the war ends affects safety in Europe and the cost of living.

levels.headline: Russia and Ukraine meet for peace talks, but no pause in the war
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine met in a city called Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. The United States helped to organise the meeting. It was the first one in nine months.
The talks did not end the war. The only clear result was that both sides swapped a large group of prisoners. A ceasefire, which would stop the fighting for a while, was not agreed. Russia's foreign minister said Russia did not want one.
American leaders said the talks were useful. One of them said that getting the two presidents to meet was like pushing a heavy rock up a hill.
The biggest problem is land. Russia wants all of a region in eastern Ukraine called Donbas, but Ukraine says no.
levels.why: The war affects people's safety and the cost of things in many countries.

levels.headline: Talks about the war in Ukraine bring no ceasefire
levels.body:
Leaders from Russia and Ukraine met in a place called Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. They were trying to talk about stopping a war. The war has gone on for a long time.
An American team helped them to talk. After two days, the countries had agreed to swap a lot of prisoners. That was good news for those families. But they did not agree to stop fighting.
Russia's foreign minister said no to a pause in the fighting. He said other European countries wanted a pause for the wrong reasons.
The biggest problem is land. Russia wants a big part of Ukraine called Donbas. Ukraine says that land belongs to Ukraine.
levels.why: Wars cause great suffering, so people hope that talks will bring peace.

levels.headline: Countries talk about stopping a war, but not yet
levels.body:
Two countries, Russia and Ukraine, have been fighting for a long time. This week they sat down in a city called Abu Dhabi to talk. A helper country, the United States, helped them.
They agreed to swap prisoners. That means each side let some people go home. That is a good thing for families who missed them.
But they did not agree to stop the fighting. They still argue about who should own a piece of land called Donbas. It is a bit like two children both saying a toy is theirs.
A helper tried to get the leaders to meet. One helper said it was like pushing a big rock up a hill.
levels.why: Talking is the first step towards stopping a war.

levels.headline: Two sides talk but cannot agree yet
levels.body:
Imagine two children who both say the same playground corner belongs to them. They argue for a long time. Then a teacher asks them to come and talk.
That is a bit like what happened this week. Two countries, Russia and Ukraine, talked in a place called Abu Dhabi. Another country, the United States, was the helper in the middle.
They agreed to let some prisoners go home, which is kind. But they did not agree to stop the fighting. One country wants the corner, and the other will not give it up.
The helper says it is hard work, like pushing a big boulder up a hill.
levels.why: Talking is a good start, but it takes time to fix a big argument.

headline: Burnham to attend UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November as rejoin question stays open

terms.meaning: An agreement where countries charge the same taxes on goods from outside and trade freely with each other.
The EU area where goods, services, money and people move freely under shared rules.
A document where a party sets out what it will do if elected.

levels.headline: Burnham to attend UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November as rejoin question stays open
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November. Items under discussion include a food and drink trade deal, progress on linking emissions trading schemes, a youth experience scheme and deeper cooperation on immigration. It remains unclear whether agreements can be reached in time.
Burnham has said that a referendum on rejoining the EU 'wouldn't be the right thing to do right now', but has declined to rule out putting one in a future Labour manifesto. He has listed options including staying as now, a customs union, the single market, or 'going all the way'. He remains committed to the 2024 manifesto, which ruled out free movement, the single market and a customs union.
The EU's foreign policy chief has said the UK should focus on joining EU defence frameworks for now. A recent YouGov survey suggested 56% of British voters would support rejoining.
levels.why: The UK's relationship with the EU affects trade, prices, travel and jobs.

levels.headline: UK-EU summit set for 20 November amid talk of closer ties
levels.body:
Andy Burnham will go to a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November. The agenda covers a food and drink trade deal, emissions trading, a youth experience scheme and closer immigration cooperation, though it is not certain deals will be ready.
The Prime Minister has said a rejoin referendum 'wouldn't be the right thing to do right now' but would not rule out a pledge in a future manifesto. He has set out choices from staying as now to a customs union, the single market or 'going all the way'. He has committed to the 2024 manifesto, which excluded free movement, the single market and a customs union.
The EU's foreign policy chief urged the UK to focus on defence cooperation first. A YouGov survey suggested 56% of voters would back rejoining.
levels.why: The summit could shape trade and travel rules affecting businesses and young people.

levels.headline: Prime Minister to meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend a summit with EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November. Talks could cover a food and drink trade deal, the carbon trading schemes of both sides, a youth experience scheme and closer cooperation on immigration. It is unclear whether any of these will be finished in time.
Burnham has said a referendum on rejoining the EU would not be right now, but has not ruled out including one in a future manifesto. He has described options from staying as things are to a customs union, the single market, or rejoining fully. He is bound by Labour's 2024 manifesto, which ruled out free movement and a customs union.
A YouGov poll suggested 56% of voters would support rejoining.
levels.why: What is agreed could change trade, travel and costs for UK businesses and families.

levels.headline: UK and EU leaders to meet on 20 November to talk trade and more
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November. They may talk about a deal on food and drink trade, a youth experience scheme, and links between their schemes for pricing carbon pollution. They also plan to talk about working together on immigration. It is not clear whether any deals will be ready.
Burnham has said holding a vote now on rejoining the EU would not be right, but he has not ruled out promising one at a future election. He has talked about a range of options, from staying as things are to rejoining fully. He has said he will keep to Labour's 2024 promises not to bring back free movement.
A poll found 56% of voters would back rejoining.
levels.why: Deals with the EU can change prices, jobs and travel for young people.

levels.headline: Prime Minister heads to Brussels to meet EU leaders
levels.body:
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, will go to Brussels on 20 November to meet EU leaders. Brussels is where the EU has its main offices. They could talk about trade in food and drink, a scheme to let young people live and work abroad, and working together on immigration.
It is not yet clear whether they will agree anything. Burnham has said that holding a vote on rejoining the EU would not be right now. But he has not ruled out putting that idea in his party's plan for a future election.
He has said he will stick to his party's 2024 promise not to bring back free movement, which lets people live and work in any EU country.
A poll found that 56% of British voters would support rejoining.
levels.why: A deal could make trade easier and give young people new chances to work abroad.

levels.headline: UK leader to meet EU leaders about trade and young people
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November. The EU is a group of European countries that work together. The UK left it in 2020, after a vote called Brexit.
They might talk about selling food and drink more easily, and a scheme that lets young people spend time abroad. They also want to talk about working together on people moving between countries. They may not agree on everything.
Mr Burnham says a vote on rejoining the EU is not right now. But he will not say it could never happen. He will keep to his party's promise not to bring back free movement.
A poll found that 56% of people would like to rejoin.
levels.why: How close the UK is to the EU changes trade, travel and prices.

levels.headline: UK and Europe to talk about closer links
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will meet leaders of the European Union on 20 November. The EU is a group of countries in Europe that work together. The UK used to be in it, but left after a vote called Brexit.
They may talk about making it easier to sell food and drink. They may also talk about letting young people go and work or study abroad for a while. It is not certain they will agree.
Some people want the UK to rejoin the EU. The Prime Minister says a vote on this is not right now, but it could come in future. A poll found that 56% of people would like to rejoin.
levels.why: How the UK works with Europe can change prices and chances for young people.

levels.headline: Meeting with our European neighbours
levels.body:
The leader of the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, will meet leaders of the European Union on 20 November. The EU is a group of nearby countries that work together as a team.
The UK left that team a few years ago. Now the leaders will talk about working together again on some things, like selling food and drink to each other, and letting young people go abroad for a while.
Some people would like the UK to join the team again. A poll found that 56 out of every 100 people would say yes. The Prime Minister says it is not the right time to vote on that, but he has not said never.
It is not sure they will agree on everything.
levels.why: Countries that work together can make it easier to trade and travel.

levels.headline: The UK and its neighbours
levels.body:
Imagine the UK is a child who left a big team of friends, called the EU. Now the two sides are going to sit down and chat. The chat is on 20 November.
They might talk about swapping snacks, which are food and drink, more easily. They might talk about letting young people visit each other. It is a bit like a school exchange trip.
Some people would like the UK to rejoin the team. The leader, called the Prime Minister, says it is not the time to ask everyone to vote. But he has not said no for ever.
They might not agree on everything, and that is okay.
levels.why: Friends can still be friendly even when they choose different teams.

levels.headline: Visiting the neighbours
levels.body:
The UK has some neighbours called the European Union, which is a group of countries that share some rules. The UK used to be one of them, but left a while ago.
On 20 November, the leader of the UK, called the Prime Minister, will go and visit them. They will talk about working together a bit more, like making it easier to trade food and drink.
Some people want the UK to join them again. The Prime Minister says now is not the time for everyone to vote on it. He says maybe later.
It is like making up after a quarrel. You can be friends again slowly.
levels.why: Friendly neighbours can help each other with trade and travel.

headline: Government sets out 'earned settlement' with a 10-year default wait to settle in the UK

terms.meaning: Permission to live in the UK permanently, without time limits on stay.
A system where people must meet conditions and wait longer before they can stay permanently.
A period when the public and groups are asked for views before a policy is decided.

levels.headline: Government sets out 'earned settlement' with a 10-year default wait to settle in the UK
levels.body:
The Government has set out an 'earned settlement' model that doubles the time many foreign workers must wait before they can settle permanently. The standard route becomes 10 years.
High earners can settle after 3 years, and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers after 5. People who have broken immigration rules face at least 20 years, and anyone who arrived by small boat or other clandestine means faces an extra 10 years.
All applicants must meet four conditions, including a clean criminal record and no debt owed to the taxpayer. Care workers earning at least £25,000 who met their visa conditions can settle after 5 years, a concession after pushback from unions and some Labour figures. Those already settled are unaffected.
The changes follow a consultation with over 200,000 responses and are reported to take effect next year. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK had 'lost control of immigration' after Brexit and backed Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood. Reform has pledged to scrap indefinite leave to remain.
levels.why: The rules decide who can build a permanent life in the UK, and shape the workforce in the NHS and care.

levels.headline: New settlement rules double the usual wait to 10 years
levels.body:
Ministers have announced an 'earned settlement' system under which many foreign workers will wait twice as long before they can settle permanently. The default is now 10 years.
High earners can settle in 3 years, and some public service workers, including doctors, nurses and teachers, in 5. Those who have breached immigration rules face at least 20 years, and people who arrived by small boat or other clandestine route face an additional 10.
Everyone must meet four conditions, including a spotless criminal record and no debts to the taxpayer. Care workers earning at least £25,000 can settle after 5 years, a concession made after criticism from unions and some Labour MPs. People who already have settled status are not affected.
The plan followed a consultation with more than 200,000 responses and is reportedly due next year. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the country had 'lost control of immigration', while Reform has pledged to abolish indefinite leave to remain.
levels.why: The rules affect migrant workers, employers and public services such as the NHS.

levels.headline: Migrants to wait longer to settle in the UK under new Government plan
levels.body:
The Government has unveiled an 'earned settlement' model that will double the usual wait for many foreign workers who want to settle in the UK for good. The normal route will now take 10 years.
High earners can settle within 3 years, and some doctors, nurses and teachers within 5. Anyone who has broken immigration rules must wait at least 20 years, and people who arrived by small boat or similar routes face an extra 10.
Applicants must also meet four conditions, such as having no criminal record and owing no debt to the taxpayer. After criticism from unions and some Labour figures, care workers earning at least £25,000 will be able to settle after 5 years. Existing settled status is not affected.
More than 200,000 people responded to a consultation. The rules are reportedly due to start next year. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain had 'lost control of immigration'.
levels.why: This could change who stays in the UK long term and who fills jobs in key services.

levels.headline: New rules make people wait longer to stay in the UK for good
levels.body:
The UK Government has announced new rules for people from abroad who want to settle in the UK permanently. Under a plan called 'earned settlement', the usual wait will double to 10 years.
Some people can settle faster. High earners can do so in 3 years, and some public service workers, such as doctors, nurses and teachers, in 5. People who have broken immigration rules must wait at least 20 years, and those who came by small boat must wait an extra 10.
Everyone must meet four conditions, including no criminal record and no debts owed to the taxpayer. Care workers who earn at least £25,000 can settle after 5 years. People who have already settled are not affected.
The plan is reported to start next year. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the country had 'lost control of immigration'.
levels.why: It affects who can build a permanent life in the UK and who works in jobs like care.

levels.headline: UK to double the wait for many migrants to settle permanently
levels.body:
The Government has said many people who come to work in the UK will have to wait longer before they can settle here permanently. Settling means being allowed to stay for good. The normal wait will double to 10 years under a plan called 'earned settlement'.
Some people will have a shorter wait. People on high pay can settle after 3 years. Some doctors, nurses and teachers can settle after 5 years. People who broke the rules will wait at least 20 years. Anyone who came by small boat will wait an extra 10 years.
All applicants must also meet four conditions, including having no criminal record and owing no money to the taxpayer. Care workers who earn at least £25,000 can settle after 5 years.
The changes are reported to start next year.
levels.why: Many families and workers will need to plan for a longer wait.

levels.headline: New rules mean a longer wait to live in the UK for good
levels.body:
The Government has made new rules for people who move to the UK and want to stay for good. The wait before they can do that will now be 10 years for most people. Before, it was about half that.
Some people can wait for less time. People who are paid a lot can stay after 3 years. Some doctors, nurses and teachers can stay after 5 years. People who broke the rules will wait at least 20 years. People who came across the sea in small boats will wait 10 years longer.
Everyone must also have no crime record and owe no money to the taxpayer. Care workers who earn at least £25,000 can stay after 5 years.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the country had 'lost control' of who comes in. The rules should begin next year.
levels.why: The new rules decide who can make their home in the UK for good.

levels.headline: Longer wait to stay in the UK for good
levels.body:
The Government has changed the rules for people who come from other countries to live in the UK. They want to stay here for good one day. The wait for most people will now be 10 years.
Some people wait less time. People who earn a lot wait 3 years. Some doctors, nurses and teachers wait 5 years. People who broke the rules wait at least 20 years.
People also have to show they have not broken the law and do not owe the government money. Care workers who earn at least £25,000 can wait just 5 years.
People who are already allowed to stay for good will not be affected. The new rules are meant to start next year.
levels.why: Rules like this change the lives of families who move to a new country.

levels.headline: New rules about who can stay in the UK
levels.body:
The UK has made new rules for people who move here from other countries. Some people want to live here for the rest of their lives. The rules say how long they must wait first.
For most people, the wait is now 10 years. That is a long time. People who earn a lot of money wait 3 years. Doctors, nurses and teachers might wait 5 years. People who broke the rules must wait 20 years.
People also have to show they have been good and do not owe money to the government. People who are already allowed to stay will not have to change anything.
The leader of the country, called the Prime Minister, said the country needs better control of who comes in.
levels.why: The rules decide how long families must wait to make a new country their home.

levels.headline: Waiting for a new home
levels.body:
Imagine you move to a new school. You want to join the football team for good, but the team says you must wait before you can join. Now the wait is longer than it was.
That is a bit like the new rules in the UK. When people move here from other countries, they have to wait before they can stay for ever. For most people, the wait is now 10 years. Some wait less, like doctors, nurses and teachers. Some wait more if they broke the rules.
The leaders of the country say this is fair. Others think it is too long. They are still talking about it.
The rules should start next year.
levels.why: Rules about moving countries are a big deal for families.

levels.headline: Rules for joining the UK for good
levels.body:
Think of a club. If you want to be a member for good, the club says you must wait and follow its rules. In the UK, there is a club-like rule for people who move here from other countries.
The wait to stay for ever is now 10 years for most people. That is longer than before. Doctors and nurses may wait only 5 years, because we need them. People who break the rules wait longer.
The leader, the Prime Minister, said the country had lost control of who comes in. Some people think the new rules are fair. Others think they are too hard.
The new rules should start next year.
levels.why: Moving to a new country is a big step for any family.

headline: Poland mourns after Krakow Main Market Square shooting that left six dead

terms.meaning: Violence used to frighten the public or push a political aim.
Lawyers who decide whether to bring criminal charges and lead cases in court.
A peaceful walk without chanting, held to remember victims.

levels.headline: Poland mourns after Krakow Main Market Square shooting that left six dead
levels.body:
A gunman opened fire in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday 7 November, and Euronews reported six people dead. About 15 or 16 were wounded, depending on the source, including two police officers.
Police named the suspect as Michał Oksiński, a 24-year-old Polish citizen (some reports say 25), who had no previous convictions. Officers found the bodies of three of his relatives in the flat where he lived. He died in hospital early on Monday 9 November.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the attack terrorism and prosecutors treated it as a terrorist offence. Officials first pointed to far-right ideology but later appeared to step back, and the justice minister said the investigation would establish whether he acted alone or was inspired by a group.
The square reopened on Sunday, and Poland's president and prime minister joined a silent march for the victims.
levels.why: Attacks in public places raise questions about security and how societies respond.

levels.headline: Six killed in shooting in Krakow's historic square
levels.body:
A masked man in military-style clothing drove onto Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday 7 November and opened fire, Euronews reported. Six people were reported dead and around 15 or 16 were wounded, including two police officers.
Police identified the suspect as Michał Oksiński, a 24-year-old Polish citizen, though some sources give 25. Three relatives' bodies were found in his flat. He died in hospital on Monday.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it terrorism. Early comments pointing to far-right ideology were softened, and the justice minister said investigators would test whether he acted alone or was inspired by any group.
The square reopened on Sunday 8 November. Poland's president and prime minister walked in a silent march to remember the victims.
levels.why: It shows how quickly everyday places can be hit and why investigations take time.

levels.headline: Poland in shock after deadly shooting in Krakow
levels.body:
A gunman wearing military-style clothing and a mask drove a car onto Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday 7 November and began shooting, according to Euronews. Six people were reported dead and 15 or 16 injured, including two police officers.
The suspect was named as Michał Oksiński, a 24-year-old Polish citizen with no previous convictions. Police found the bodies of three relatives in his flat. He died in hospital on Monday morning.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the attack as terrorism. Officials first suggested far-right motives but later appeared to retreat, and the justice minister said investigators were still working out whether he acted alone.
On Sunday the square reopened, and Poland's president and prime minister joined a silent march.
levels.why: The case raises questions about security and about what drove the attacker.

levels.headline: Gunman kills six in Krakow's Main Market Square
levels.body:
A man in a mask and army-style clothes drove a car onto the busy Main Market Square in Krakow, Poland, on Saturday 7 November. He then opened fire, Euronews reported. Six people died and around 15 or 16 were hurt, including two police officers.
Police said the suspect was Michał Oksiński, a 24-year-old Polish man. He had no criminal record. Police also found the bodies of three of his relatives in his flat. He died in hospital on Monday.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it terrorism. At first, officials said he held far-right views, but they later seemed less sure. The justice minister said police would look into whether he acted alone.
The square opened again on Sunday, and leaders took part in a silent march.
levels.why: Public attacks make people think about safety and how to prevent them.

levels.headline: A deadly shooting shocks the city of Krakow in Poland
levels.body:
On Saturday 7 November, a man in a mask drove a car into the main square in the city of Krakow, in Poland. Then he began to shoot. Six people died and about 15 or 16 were hurt. Two of the hurt people were police officers.
The police said the man was called Michał Oksiński. He was 24 years old and from Poland. The police also found three people from his family dead in his flat. He died in hospital on Monday.
The Polish Prime Minister, Donald Tusk, said it was an act of terrorism. Police are still finding out why it happened and whether anyone helped him.
On Sunday the square opened again. The country's president and prime minister took part in a quiet walk to remember the victims.
levels.why: People gather to remember those who were lost and to support each other.

levels.headline: Shooting in a busy square in Poland
levels.body:
On Saturday 7 November, there was a terrible attack in the main square of Krakow, a city in Poland. A man drove a car into the square and began shooting. Six people died and many more were hurt, including two police officers.
The police said the man was 24 and from Poland. He had never been in trouble with the police before. Police also found the bodies of three of his family members in his flat. He later died in hospital.
The country's leader, Donald Tusk, said it was terrorism. That means a crime meant to scare many people. Police are still trying to learn why he did it and if anyone helped.
On Sunday, leaders joined a silent walk to remember the people who died.
levels.why: The attack has shocked people in Poland and around Europe.

levels.headline: A sad attack in a city square in Poland
levels.body:
A very sad thing happened in the city of Krakow in Poland on Saturday 7 November. A man drove into a busy square and used a gun. Six people died. Many others were hurt, including two police officers.
The man was 24 years old. He had never been in trouble with the police. He died in hospital two days later. Police also found three people from his family dead in his home.
The leader of Poland, Donald Tusk, said it was an act of terrorism. This means someone hurts people to scare others. The police are now looking into why he did it.
On Sunday, people walked quietly through the city to remember those who died.
levels.why: People come together to remember those who were hurt or lost.

levels.headline: A frightening day in a Polish city
levels.body:
A frightening thing happened in a Polish city called Krakow. On a Saturday, a man went to a busy square where many people were walking. He used a gun and hurt many people. Six of them died.
The police found out who he was. He was 24 years old. He died in hospital two days later. The police are still working out why he did it.
The leader of Poland said it was an act of terrorism, which is when someone tries to scare lots of people.
On the next day, the square opened again. Leaders and many people walked quietly together to remember those who died. They wanted to show they care about each other.
levels.why: When something sad happens, people can help each other by being kind.

levels.headline: A sad day in a Polish square
levels.body:
Sometimes something very sad happens in the world. In a city called Krakow, in Poland, a man hurt many people in a busy square. Six people died.
The police are working very hard to find out why this happened. They are the helpers whose job is to keep people safe.
On the next day, the square opened again. The grown-ups of the city walked together very quietly. They did this to say they were thinking of the people who were lost and of their families.
When sad things happen, it helps to be near people who care about you.
levels.why: Being kind and staying together can help when something sad happens.

levels.headline: When people feel sad together
levels.body:
Sometimes people far away have a very sad day. In a city called Krakow, in Poland, a bad thing happened in a square where people walk and shop. Some people were hurt, and some died.
Police and other helpers came to look after everybody. They are working to find out what happened. Their job is to keep us safe.
The next day, the leaders and lots of people walked quietly together in the city. They did it to show they cared and were thinking of everyone who was sad.
If you hear sad news, it is okay to feel sad. Talking to a grown-up you trust can help.
levels.why: Caring for each other helps us feel safer when sad things happen.

headline: Israel's president asks Gadi Eisenkot to form a government after inconclusive election, a setback for Netanyahu

terms.meaning: Israel's parliament, with 120 seats.
A government formed by several parties that agree to work together.
Official permission to try to form a government.

levels.headline: Israel's president asks Gadi Eisenkot to form a government after inconclusive election, a setback for Netanyahu
levels.body:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog asked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party, to try to form the next government on 7 November, a setback for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Factions with 67 Knesset members backed Eisenkot and 46 backed Netanyahu.
Neither side won the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 27 October election. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has 28 days to build a coalition, which can be extended by up to 14 days. He would probably need Arab-led parties, which have joined a governing coalition only once in Israel's history, and some potential partners object to relying on them.
On Iran, Eisenkot shares Netanyahu's hard line, so analysts say policy on Iran, the Palestinians and security may change little. Netanyahu's Likud alleged fraud and foreign interference in the vote, but the election commission said no fraud was found.
levels.why: Who governs Israel affects the war in Gaza, tensions with Iran and the wider Middle East.

levels.headline: Eisenkot given first chance to replace Netanyahu
levels.body:
President Isaac Herzog on 7 November tasked Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, with forming Israel's next government. It is a setback for Benjamin Netanyahu. Factions with 67 members of the Knesset backed Eisenkot, while 46 backed Netanyahu.
The 27 October election left neither bloc with the 61 seats needed. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a coalition, extendable by up to 14, and will probably need Arab-led parties, who have been in a governing coalition just once. Some possible partners dislike that idea.
Both men take a hard line on Iran, so one analysis suggests policy on Iran and security may not shift much. Likud alleged fraud, but the election commission found none.
levels.why: The outcome shapes Israel's approach to Gaza, Iran and relations with its neighbours.

levels.headline: Israeli president turns to Netanyahu's rival to form a government
levels.body:
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked Gadi Eisenkot to try to form the next government. Eisenkot leads the Yashar party and used to head the army. The decision on 7 November is a setback for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In all, 67 members of parliament backed Eisenkot and 46 backed Netanyahu.
Neither side won a majority of 61 seats in the 27 October election. Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible extension of up to 14. He would likely need parties led by Arab citizens, who have been in a governing coalition only once, and some partners are uneasy.
On Iran, both men are hawkish. The election commission found no fraud, despite claims from Netanyahu's Likud.
levels.why: The next Israeli government will influence the Gaza conflict and tensions with Iran.

levels.headline: Netanyahu's rival is asked to build Israel's next government
levels.body:
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a new government. Eisenkot is a former army chief who leads the Yashar party. This is bad news for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Members of parliament backed Eisenkot by 67 to 46.
In the 27 October election, neither side won the 61 seats needed to form a majority. Eisenkot now has 28 days to put together a coalition, which means a group of parties that agree to govern together. He can get up to 14 more days. He would probably need parties led by Arab citizens, who have joined a government only once before.
Both men are tough on Iran.
levels.why: The government Israel ends up with will affect peace efforts and tension across the region.

levels.headline: Israel's president asks a new leader to try to form a government
levels.body:
Israel held an election on 27 October, but no group won enough seats to rule alone. A party needs 61 of the 120 seats to have a majority. On 7 November, the president, Isaac Herzog, asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a government.
Eisenkot used to lead the army and now leads a party called Yashar. More members of parliament supported him, 67, than supported the current Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who got 46.
Eisenkot has 28 days to find partners, and he may get up to 14 more. He will probably need parties led by Arab citizens, which is rare. The election commission said there was no cheating in the vote.
levels.why: The new government will make big choices about the war and peace in the region.

levels.headline: Israel may get a new leader after an unclear election
levels.body:
Israel held an election on 27 October. No party or group won a majority. That means no one had enough seats to run the country alone. A majority is 61 out of 120 seats.
On 7 November, the president, Isaac Herzog, asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a new government. He used to be in charge of Israel's army. More politicians supported him than supported the Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Now Eisenkot has 28 days to find enough partners. He may get more time if he needs it. Some of the partners he may need are parties led by Arab citizens. That has happened only once before.
levels.why: Who runs Israel can change what happens in a very tense part of the world.

levels.headline: Israel's leaders are choosing who will run the country
levels.body:
Israel had an election on 27 October. Nobody won enough votes to run the country alone. So, the president asked a man named Gadi Eisenkot to try to put together a new government.
A government needs at least 61 out of 120 seats in parliament. Eisenkot used to be the head of the army. More politicians said they would back him than said they would back Benjamin Netanyahu, who is the Prime Minister now.
Eisenkot has 28 days to find partners. He may have a little more time if he needs it. If he cannot do it, Israel may have to choose again.
levels.why: The leaders of Israel make choices that can matter far beyond Israel.

levels.headline: Israel needs a new team to lead
levels.body:
Israel had a vote to choose its leaders. But no one won by enough. It is a bit like a game where nobody has scored enough points to win.
So the president asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a team that can lead the country. A team like this is called a government. He needs lots of people to join him.
He has 28 days to find enough friends to join. The man who leads now, Benjamin Netanyahu, would like to stay as leader, but the president picked Eisenkot to go first.
If Eisenkot cannot find enough friends, it will be someone else's turn.
levels.why: Countries pick leaders by voting, and sometimes they need to talk to find a team.

levels.headline: Choosing a team captain
levels.body:
Imagine your class picks a captain for the football team. Some children want one person, and some want another. Nobody gets enough votes. So the teacher asks one child to go and try to find enough friends who agree.
That is a bit like what happened in Israel. There was a vote, and no one won by enough. The president asked a man named Gadi Eisenkot to see if he could gather enough friends to be the leader.
He has 28 days to try. If he finds enough friends, he leads. If not, someone else gets a turn.
Voting and talking are how countries pick who leads them.
levels.why: Picking a leader fairly often means a lot of talking.

levels.headline: Picking someone to lead
levels.body:
Sometimes a group cannot agree who should be in charge. The grown-ups in Israel had a vote, and no one got enough votes to be the boss.
So the person in charge of choosing, called the president, picked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try first. He has to find enough people who say yes to him. He has 28 days.
It is a bit like asking friends to join your team in the playground. You need enough friends to play the game.
If he cannot find enough friends, someone else will have a turn.
levels.why: Countries choose leaders by asking people, and it can take time.

headline: Oil prices fall back as markets weigh hopes of an Iran deal against stalled nuclear talks

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil, quoted in dollars per barrel.
The standard unit for oil, about 159 litres.
Uranium processed to a higher purity, which can be used for power or, at very high levels, for weapons.

levels.headline: Oil prices fall back as markets weigh hopes of an Iran deal against stalled nuclear talks
levels.body:
Oil prices have dropped sharply since the US midterm elections as investors weigh hopes of a diplomatic end to the Iran war. Brent crude fell below $90 a barrel for the first time since August, and CNBC reported it down 6.9% for the week after losing 16.4% the week before. Trading Economics showed crude at $86.15 on 12 November, down 0.44% on the day.
Prices have bounced at times and remain well above a year ago. A key obstacle remains: Iran has said it will not surrender its enriched nuclear material.
The wider effect is on inflation. The Bank of England has said the energy shock from the Middle East conflict is the main driver behind inflation that it expects to reach about 5% by mid-2027. In the US, energy remains a worry for the Fed, with Governor Christopher Waller warning that earlier energy shocks may keep affecting prices into 2027.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and food costs and so into interest rates.

levels.headline: Crude slides on hopes of diplomacy with Iran
levels.body:
Oil has fallen sharply since the US midterms as investors bet on a diplomatic end to the Iran war. Brent crude dropped below $90 a barrel for the first time since August, and CNBC said it was down 6.9% for the week after a 16.4% fall the week before. Trading Economics put crude at $86.15 on 12 November.
Prices have bounced at times and are still well above a year ago. Iran has said it will not hand over its enriched nuclear material, a major obstacle to a deal.
Lower oil would ease pressure on inflation. The Bank of England blames the energy shock for inflation it expects to near 5% by mid-2027, and Fed governor Christopher Waller has warned energy shocks could affect US prices into 2027.
levels.why: Oil costs reach households through fuel, transport and heating bills.

levels.headline: Oil prices drop as investors hope for an end to the Iran conflict
levels.body:
Oil prices have fallen sharply this month as investors hope the Iran war can be settled by talks. Brent crude went below $90 a barrel for the first time since August. CNBC reported a 6.9% weekly fall after a 16.4% drop the week before. Trading Economics showed crude at $86.15 on 12 November.
The price has recovered at times and remains well above where it was a year ago. Iran has said it will not give up its enriched nuclear material, which is a key obstacle in the talks.
The fall matters for inflation. The Bank of England says the energy shock is the main reason it expects UK inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027. A Fed governor, Christopher Waller, has also warned that energy effects could last into 2027.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can ease the cost of living, but the gains may not last.

levels.headline: Oil gets cheaper as people hope for a deal with Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil has fallen a lot since the US midterm elections. Investors hope the war involving Iran can end through talks. Brent crude, the main world price, went below $90 a barrel for the first time since August. It fell 6.9% in one week, after a 16.4% fall the week before. On 12 November, crude was about $86 a barrel.
The price has bounced up at times, and it is still well above where it was a year ago. Iran says it will not give up its enriched nuclear material, which is a big problem for the talks.
This matters because oil costs affect petrol and heating. The Bank of England says the energy shock is behind its warning that UK inflation could reach about 5% by mid-2027.
levels.why: Oil prices affect what we pay for petrol, heating and shopping.

levels.headline: Oil prices drop as people hope for peace talks with Iran
levels.body:
Oil prices have dropped over the past couple of weeks. People who buy and sell oil hope that talks can end the war with Iran. The main world price, called Brent crude, went below $90 a barrel for the first time since August. A barrel is the standard amount of oil that is bought and sold. On 12 November the price was about $86.
The price has gone up and down, and it is still much higher than a year ago. Iran says it will not give up its special nuclear material, which makes a deal harder.
Oil matters to everyone. When it costs more, petrol and heating can cost more too. The Bank of England thinks this could push UK prices up by about 5% by the middle of 2027.
levels.why: Oil costs touch fuel, heating and the price of everyday things.

levels.headline: Oil costs less, but the worry has not gone away
levels.body:
The price of oil has gone down a lot in recent weeks. Many people hope that talks will end the war with Iran. Oil is a liquid fuel that is used for petrol and for making many things. The main world price went below $90 a barrel, and it was about $86 on 12 November.
The price still goes up and down. And it is higher than a year ago. Iran says it will not give up some special nuclear material. This makes it hard to make a deal.
When oil costs more, shops and drivers pay more, and prices can rise for everyone. The Bank of England thinks prices in the UK could rise by about 5% by the middle of 2027.
levels.why: What oil costs affects almost everything we buy.

levels.headline: Oil prices go down as people hope for peace
levels.body:
The price of oil has gone down in the past few weeks. People hope that a war involving Iran might end soon. Oil is used to make petrol for cars and to heat some buildings.
The price went below $90 for a barrel of oil, and on 12 November it was about $86. A barrel is a big container of oil. A year ago, the price was a lot lower than now.
Iran says it will not hand over some special nuclear material. This makes it harder to agree on peace.
When oil costs more, many other things cost more too. When it costs less, that can help families.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can mean cheaper petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil gets cheaper
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars and lorries. The price of oil has gone down lately. People hope a war might end soon.
One big barrel of oil costs about $86 now. A week ago it cost more. But it is still more than it was a year ago.
When oil costs less, petrol can cost less too. Food can cost less because lorries use less money to carry it.
A country called Iran has said it will not give up some things that worry other countries. So the war is not over yet.
levels.why: When oil is cheaper, many things we need can cost less.

levels.headline: Why oil prices matter
levels.body:
Think of oil as the juice that makes cars and lorries go. When the juice costs more, it costs more to drive and to carry food to shops. Then the shops put up their prices a little.
In the last few weeks, the price of oil has gone down. People hope that a war might end soon. When people feel calmer, the price goes down.
But the war is not over yet, so the price could go up again. It is a bit like the price of a toy that keeps changing in the shop window.
When oil is cheaper, families can sometimes spend less on petrol.
levels.why: The price of oil can change how much we pay for lots of things.

levels.headline: Juice for cars
levels.body:
Cars, lorries and trains need something to make them go. A lot of the time that is a thing called oil. People buy and sell oil all over the world.
The price of oil changes all the time. Lately, it has gone down. That is because people hope a war might end soon.
When oil costs less, it can cost less to get food to the shops, and it can cost less to drive a car. That helps families.
But the price can change again. It is like the price of sweets that keeps going up and down.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can help families spend less on petrol.

headline: UK unemployment stood at 4.9% in the latest official figures, with new ONS data due on 17 November

terms.meaning: The share of people who are looking for work and able to start, out of everyone who is working or looking.
The Office for National Statistics, the UK's official statistics body.
The share of people aged 16 to 64 who are in work.

levels.headline: UK unemployment stood at 4.9% in the latest official figures, with new ONS data due on 17 November
levels.body:
The most recent official figures from the Office for National Statistics, published on 20 October, put the UK unemployment rate at 4.9% for June to August 2026. The employment rate rose slightly and the unemployment rate fell a little in the quarter.
The next labour market release is due on 17 November. It will be watched closely because the Bank of England raised interest rates by 0.25 points to 4% on 5 November and expects inflation to climb to about 5% by mid-2027. A weak jobs market could strengthen arguments against further rises.
