The ONS figures are based on a survey, and one other data provider listed an older unemployment reading of 4.7% that conflicts with the ONS figure. The ONS number is the one used here. This summary does not include wage growth because that figure could not be verified.
levels.why: Jobs figures help to shape interest rates, pay and how secure workers feel.

levels.headline: Unemployment 4.9% in latest ONS data, with new figures due on 17 November
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics reported on 20 October that UK unemployment was 4.9% in the three months to August 2026. The employment rate edged up and the unemployment rate edged down.
New figures are due on 17 November. They matter because the Bank of England raised its rate by 0.25 points to 4% on 5 November and says inflation could near 5% by mid-2027. Weak jobs data could argue against further rises.
The ONS estimates come from a survey. One data provider showed an earlier reading of 4.7%, which conflicts with the ONS figure, so the ONS number is used. Wage growth is not covered because it could not be verified.
levels.why: The jobs market affects pay, spending and what the Bank of England does next.

levels.headline: Jobs market in focus as new unemployment figures approach
levels.body:
The latest official figures show UK unemployment at 4.9% in the three months to August 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics. The employment rate rose slightly and unemployment fell a little.
The next figures are published on 17 November. Economists will watch them because the Bank of England has just raised interest rates to 4% and expects inflation to rise to about 5% by the middle of 2027. If the jobs market weakens, that could make further rate rises less likely.
The ONS figures come from a survey. A separate website listed an older figure of 4.7%, which did not match, so the ONS number is used here. Pay data is not included, as it could not be confirmed.
levels.why: Unemployment affects how safe jobs feel and how much people spend.

levels.headline: UK unemployment is 4.9%, and new figures are coming
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics, the UK's official number-counting body, says unemployment was 4.9% between June and August 2026. That means about 5 in every 100 people who wanted a job did not have one. The share of people in work went up a little, and unemployment went down a little.
New figures are due on 17 November. They will be watched because the Bank of England has just raised interest rates to 4%. It expects prices to rise by about 5% a year by mid-2027.
If fewer people have jobs, the Bank may be less keen to raise rates again. The ONS figures come from a survey, so they are estimates. We could not confirm wage figures.
levels.why: Job figures show how the economy is doing and what may happen to rates.

levels.headline: About 5 in every 100 people looking for work cannot find a job
levels.body:
New official numbers show that 4.9% of people in the UK who wanted to work could not find a job between June and August 2026. That is almost 5 in every 100 people. The group that counts these numbers is called the Office for National Statistics, or ONS.
A few more people were in work than before, and a few fewer were without a job.
The ONS will publish new numbers on 17 November. People will look at them because the Bank of England has just raised interest rates. It thinks prices could rise by about 5% in a year by the middle of 2027.
The numbers come from a survey, so they are close guesses rather than exact counts.
levels.why: If more people have jobs, families can feel safer about paying bills.

levels.headline: Almost 5 in every 100 workers are looking for work
levels.body:
New numbers from the Office for National Statistics show that 4.9% of people who wanted a job did not have one between June and August 2026. That is nearly 5 in every 100 people.
A few more people had jobs than before, and a few fewer were looking for work.
The ONS will share new numbers on 17 November. Many people are watching because the Bank of England has just raised interest rates, which makes borrowing cost more. The Bank thinks prices will keep rising.
The numbers come from asking lots of people questions, so they are good guesses, not perfect counts.
levels.why: Having a job helps people pay for their homes and food.

levels.headline: How many people do not have a job?
levels.body:
Every few weeks, a group called the Office for National Statistics counts how many people in the UK want a job but cannot find one. The newest number says it is 4.9%. That is almost 5 out of every 100 people.
A few more people had jobs than before, and a few fewer were looking. So things got a tiny bit better.
The group will share new numbers on 17 November. Grown-ups will look at them closely because the bank that helps look after the UK's money has just made borrowing cost more.
The group asks lots of people questions to work this out, so the number is a good guess.
levels.why: Having a job helps people look after their families.

levels.headline: Counting people who want a job
levels.body:
Some grown-ups want a job but cannot find one. A group called the ONS counts them. The newest count says it is about 5 out of every 100 people.
That is a small number but it matters. Having a job means you can pay for food, a home and fun things for your family.
The group will count again soon, on 17 November, and say if it has changed.
They do not ask every single person. They ask lots of people and use the answers to make a very good guess.
levels.why: Jobs let families buy the things they need.

levels.headline: Grown-ups who need jobs
levels.body:
Grown-ups go to work to earn money. Money is how they buy food, clothes and toys. Some grown-ups want a job but cannot find one yet. That is hard for them.
A group counted how many grown-ups were looking for work. About 5 out of every 100 were. If your class had 100 grown-ups, about 5 would be looking for a job.
A few more people had jobs than before, so that is a little good news.
The group will count again soon to see if it changes.
levels.why: Work gives families the money to look after each other.

levels.headline: Looking for a job
levels.body:
When you grow up, you may go to work. People work to earn money so they can buy food and a home. Some people look for a job for a while before they find one.
A group of people counted how many grown-ups in the UK were looking for a job. It was about 5 out of every 100. Imagine a class of 100 grown-ups. Five of them would be looking for work.
They will count again soon to see if it changes.
When more people have jobs, more families can buy what they need.
levels.why: Work helps people feel safe and happy at home.
